---
name: docs-drift-check
description: Audit a repository's documentation (README, CONTRIBUTING, docs folder) against the actual code and list every statement that is no longer true, with file-and-line evidence. Writes DRIFT_REPORT.md and DRIFT_REPORT.json. Use when asked to check, audit or verify docs for drift or outdated content.

# DocDrift: documentation drift audit

Goal: find every place where the documentation says something the code no longer supports,
prove it with evidence, and write one clear report for humans (Markdown) and one for tools
(JSON, used by the DocDrift dashboard).

Keep costs low. Do not re-read files you have already read. Use read-only `explore`
subagents for checking (they run on a lighter model and cannot change files).

<Steps>
<Step>
**Find the target.** The target folder is the folder the user names (for example
`audits/flask-realworld-example-app`). If none is named, the target is the workspace root.
All paths in the report are written relative to the target folder.
Never audit the DocDrift tool's own files (`.bob/`, `dashboard/`, `benchmark/`, `bob_sessions/`)
unless the target folder is the workspace root and the user asked for it.
</Step>

<Step>
**Find the docs.** If the user named doc files, audit only those. Otherwise audit, in order:
README (any of README.md, README.rst, README.txt, README), CONTRIBUTING, other top-level
.md/.rst files, then a docs/ folder if it is small (at most 10 files; otherwise only the
README and CONTRIBUTING, and say so in the report). Skip CHANGELOG, LICENSE, auto-generated
API reference and anything in node_modules, vendor, venv, .venv, bin, obj, dist, build, .git.
</Step>

<Step>
**Record the licence.** Read the LICENSE file (or the "license" field of package.json,
pyproject.toml or setup.cfg) and record the licence name, for example MIT or Apache-2.0.
If none is found, record "NOT FOUND". This matters because only permissively licensed
projects may be used in the hackathon.
</Step>

<Step>
**Extract claims.** Read the docs and pull out every statement that can be checked
against the code. Sort each one into a category from `categories.md`:
COMMAND, PATH, ENV, API, VERSION, DEPENDENCY, COUNT.
Give each claim an ID (C1, C2, ...) and record the doc file and line it came from.
Ignore opinions, marketing text and things that cannot be checked from the repo.
Write the claim list into your todo list so progress is visible.
</Step>

<Step>
**Check claims in parallel.** Spawn one read-only `explore` subagent per category
that has claims (up to six). Give each subagent:
- the target folder,
- the list of claims in its category (ID, exact quoted text, doc location), and
- the checking rules for that category from `categories.md`.

Each subagent must return, for every claim, one verdict:
- OK: the code confirms it (cite file:line),
- DRIFT: the code contradicts it (cite file:line and say what the truth is),
- UNVERIFIED: no clear evidence either way (say what was searched).

If there are fewer than 5 claims in total, check them directly instead of spawning subagents.
Also run the ENV reverse check from `categories.md` (settings the code reads that the docs
never mention), even if there are no ENV claims.
</Step>

<Step>
**Double-check every DRIFT.** Before reporting a DRIFT:
1. Re-open the cited code evidence yourself and confirm it. If it is weak, downgrade the
   claim to UNVERIFIED. A false alarm is worse than a missed problem.
2. Re-open the doc file and confirm the quoted text is on exactly the cited line number.
   Line numbers start at 1. If the quote is on a different line, correct the number.
</Step>

<Step>
**Group by root cause.** If several DRIFT claims come from the same underlying problem
(for example a missing file that is mentioned in two places), report them as ONE finding
and list all the affected claim IDs and doc lines in it. Each claim still counts
separately in the trust score.
</Step>

<Step>
**Rate severity** for each finding using `categories.md`:
HIGH (a new developer following the docs will fail), MEDIUM (confusing or misleading),
LOW (cosmetic or minor).
</Step>

<Step>
**Write the reports** into the target folder:
1. `DRIFT_REPORT.md`, using exactly the layout in `report-template.md`.
2. `DRIFT_REPORT.json`, using exactly the structure in `report-schema.md`.
   For `audited_at`, use today's date from your environment details (YYYY-MM-DD). Never guess a
   date; if you do not know it, write null. It must be valid
   JSON (double quotes, no comments, no trailing commas) and contain the same numbers and
   findings as the Markdown report.

Trust score = OK claims / (OK + DRIFT claims) x 100, rounded to a whole number.
UNVERIFIED claims are listed but not counted in the score. If there are no OK or DRIFT
claims at all, the score is null.
</Step>

<Step>
**Finish** with a short chat summary: target, licence, number of claims checked, DRIFT
findings by severity, and the trust score. If you were started as a subtask, return this
summary as your result so the Pilot can use it.
</Step>
</Steps>

1 | # Claim categories and how to check them
2 | 
3 | ## COMMAND
4 | Shell commands the docs tell people to run (install, build, test, start, migrate).
5 | Check:
6 | - npm / yarn / pnpm scripts exist in package.json "scripts".
7 | - make targets exist in the Makefile.
8 | - dotnet commands point to real .csproj / .sln files and projects.
9 | - python commands point to real modules or scripts; pip install uses real requirement files.
10 | - docker / docker compose commands point to real Dockerfiles, compose files and service names.
11 | - Flags and arguments are still accepted by the script, if the script is in the repo.
12 | 
13 | ## PATH
14 | Files and folders the docs mention (config files, entry points, folders to edit).
15 | Check: the path exists exactly as written (case matters). If not, search for a file
16 | with the same name elsewhere. If one is found, it was probably moved: report the new path.
17 | A PATH claim only needs the file or folder to exist. If a file is listed by a directory
18 | listing or glob but its contents are blocked (for example by .bobignore), it still
19 | exists: mark the claim OK, not UNVERIFIED.
20 | 
21 | ## COUNT
22 | Numbers the docs state about the code ("68 tests", "5 endpoints", "3 models").
23 | Check: count carefully, and watch for things that multiply the count.
24 | For tests in particular, @pytest.mark.parametrize, test classes, and fixtures with
25 | params make the real number of tests larger than the number of `def test_` lines.
26 | If any of these are present and you cannot run the test collector, mark the claim
27 | UNVERIFIED and explain why, instead of reporting DRIFT from a simple text count.
28 | 
29 | ## ENV
30 | Environment variables and config keys (DATABASE_URL, PORT, API keys, appsettings keys).
31 | Check:
32 | - Search the code for where the variable is read (process.env, os.environ, os.getenv,
33 |   Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable, IConfiguration keys, .env.example).
34 | - DRIFT if the docs name a variable the code never reads, or if the code requires a
35 |   variable the docs setup section never mentions (report the missing one too).
36 | - Also check default values and ports if the docs state them.
37 | - ALWAYS do a reverse check, even if the docs make no ENV claims: search the code for
38 |   every environment variable and config key it reads, and list any that the docs never
39 |   mention. Record each one's name, where it is read (file:line), and its default value
40 |   if the code has one. Never read or quote the values in .env files: only the names.
41 |   This list is what the fixer needs to write correct setup instructions.
42 | - Report the undocumented settings as a DRIFT finding (not just a note) when either:
43 |   (a) a doc file, including comments in .env.example, promises that the settings are
44 |       documented ("a complete list is in the documentation") and they are not, or
45 |   (b) the code REQUIRES a setting (no default, startup fails without it) and the setup
46 |       instructions never mention it.
47 |   Otherwise list them only in the "Undocumented settings" table.
48 | 
49 | ## API
50 | Code examples, function / class names, parameters, HTTP routes and methods.
51 | Check:
52 | - Functions and classes in examples exist with the same name and parameter list.
53 | - HTTP routes exist with the same path and method (look at route decorators,
54 |   controllers, router definitions, MapGet/MapPost calls).
55 | - Request/response field names match the models.
56 | 
57 | ## VERSION
58 | Runtime and tool versions (Node 18, Python 3.11, .NET 8, Java 17).
59 | Check against: package.json "engines", .nvmrc, .python-version, pyproject.toml,
60 | global.json, TargetFramework in .csproj, Dockerfile base images, CI config files.
61 | 
62 | ## DEPENDENCY
63 | Libraries and services the docs say are needed (PostgreSQL, Redis, a specific package).
64 | Check: they appear in dependency files, docker-compose services or config.
65 | DRIFT if the docs require something the project no longer uses, or the project
66 | clearly needs something the docs never mention.
67 | 
68 | # Evidence must come from the repository
69 | 
70 | A DRIFT verdict needs evidence inside the repository (a file and line that contradicts
71 | the docs). Knowledge about the outside world (a tool release, a deprecated command, a newer
72 | library version) is NOT evidence of drift, because the docs may still match the code.
73 | List such observations separately under "Outdated practices" (advice only, never counted in
74 | the trust score, never fixed automatically), and say plainly that they come from general
75 | knowledge, not from the code.
76 | 
77 | # Severity guide
78 | 
79 | - HIGH: following the docs will fail. Examples: a setup command that does not exist,
80 |   a required env var that is missing from the docs, a wrong runtime major version.
81 | - MEDIUM: misleading or will waste time but does not block. Examples: a moved file,
82 |   an outdated code example, a renamed route in an API table.
83 | - LOW: cosmetic. Examples: a stale default value that is rarely used, wrong casing
84 |   in a path on a case-insensitive system, outdated optional steps.

7 | ## Deploy to Heroku

14 | ## Deploy on your Computer
15 | 
16 | ### Setup
17 | 
18 | Follow these steps if you want to run this application on your computer, either
19 | in a Docker container or as a standalone Python application.
20 | 
21 | ```bash
22 | git clone https://github.com/miguelgrinberg/microblog-api
23 | cd microblog-api
24 | cp .env.example .env
25 | ```
26 | 
27 | Open the new `.env` file and enter values for the configuration variables.
28 | 
29 | ### Run with Docker
30 | 
31 | To start:
32 | 
33 | ```bash
34 | docker-compose up -d
35 | ```
36 | 
37 | The application runs on port 5000 on your Docker host. You can access the API
38 | documentation on the `/docs` URL (i.e. `http://localhost:5000/docs` if you are
39 | running Docker locally).
40 | 
41 | To populate the database with some randomly generated data:
42 | 
43 | ```bash
44 | docker-compose run --rm microblog-api bash -c "flask fake users 10 && flask fake posts 100"
45 | ```
46 | 
47 | To stop the application:
48 | 
49 | ```bash
50 | docker-compose down
51 | ```
52 | 
53 | ### Run locally
54 | 
55 | Set up a Python 3 virtualenv and install the dependencies on it:
56 | 
57 | ```bash
58 | python3 -m venv venv
59 | source venv/bin/activate
60 | pip install -r requirements.txt
61 | ```
62 | 
63 | Create the database and populate it with some randomly generated data:
64 | 
65 | ```bash
66 | alembic upgrade head
67 | flask fake users 10
68 | flask fake posts 100
69 | ```
70 | 
71 | Run the application with the Flask development web server:
72 | 
73 | ```bash
74 | flask run
75 | ```
76 | 
77 | The application runs on `localhost:5000`. You can access the API documentation
78 | at `http://localhost:5000/docs`.

80 | ## Configuration
81 | 
82 | Copy `.env.example` to `.env` as a starting point, then set the variables below
83 | as needed.
84 | 
85 | | Variable | Default | Description |
86 | |---|---|---|
87 | | `DATABASE_URL` | `sqlite:///db.sqlite` | SQLAlchemy database URL |
88 | | `SQL_ECHO` | _(empty)_ | Set to `yes` to echo all SQL statements to stdout |
89 | | `SECRET_KEY` | `top-secret!` | Secret key used to sign tokens and sessions; always set your own value in production |
90 | | `DISABLE_AUTH` | _(empty)_ | Set to any non-empty value to disable token authentication |
91 | | `ACCESS_TOKEN_MINUTES` | `15` | Lifetime of an access token, in minutes |
92 | | `REFRESH_TOKEN_DAYS` | `7` | Lifetime of a refresh token, in days |
93 | | `REFRESH_TOKEN_IN_COOKIE` | `yes` | Set to `yes` to return the refresh token in a cookie |
94 | | `REFRESH_TOKEN_IN_BODY` | _(empty)_ | Set to `yes` to also return the refresh token in the response body |
95 | | `RESET_TOKEN_MINUTES` | `15` | Lifetime of a password-reset token, in minutes |
96 | | `PASSWORD_RESET_URL` | `http://localhost:3000/reset` | Front-end URL that handles password resets |
97 | | `USE_CORS` | `yes` | Set to `yes` to enable CORS headers |
98 | | `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` | _(empty)_ | OAuth2 client ID for Google login |

105 | | `MAIL_PORT` | `25` | SMTP server port |

111 | ## Troubleshooting
112 | 
113 | On macOS Monterey and newer, Apple decided to use port 5000 for its AirPlay
114 | service, which means that the Microblog API server will not be able to run on
115 | this port. There are two possible ways to solve this problem:
116 | 
117 | 1. Disable the AirPlay Receiver service. To do this, open the System
118 | Preferences, go to "Sharing" and uncheck "AirPlay Receiver".
119 | 2. Move Microblog API to another port:
120 |     - If you are running Microblog API with Docker, add a
121 |     `MICROBLOG_API_PORT=4000` line to your *.env* file. Change the 4000 to your
122 |     desired port number.
123 |     - If you are running Microblog API with Python, start the server with the
124 |     command `flask run --port=4000`.
